findings.title: npm plan recording follows a predictable staging symlink
findings.summary: When recording plan operations, the npm CLI writes to a basename/PID staging path without exclusive creation. A local attacker who can create entries in that directory can redirect the write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI user.

severity.rationale: This is a local, conditional file-integrity failure: exploitation needs attacker write access to the plan directory and prediction/observation of the CLI PID. The target must be writable by the victim. These constrained prerequisites lower likelihood.
severity.changeConditions: A workflow routinely recording plans in a directory writable by less-trusted users increases likelihood. An exclusive regular staging file in a private unpredictable directory removes the link-following path.

confidence.rationale: Source directly constructs predictable partial name, calls default fs.writeFileSync and only then renames. No exclusive/no-follow protection applies; no runtime filesystem manipulation was performed.

taxonomy.category: Symlink following in temporary-file publication

codeEvidence.label: Plan recording route
codeEvidence.explanation: A normal edit with plan plus operation flags enters recordPlan.

codeEvidence.label: Predictable staging path is followed by default write
codeEvidence.explanation: Directory attacker can plant the basename/PID partial as symlink; writeFileSync follows it and truncates referent before rename.

rootCause.summary: `runEdit()` routes plan-plus-operation flags to `recordPlan()`. It derives the temporary pathname solely from target basename and process PID and calls `fs.writeFileSync()` with default truncating write semantics. A preexisting symlink at that pathname is followed, modifying its referent before `renameSync()` can publish the plan. Resolving the intended plan target does not validate the separate staging entry.

findings.remediation: Create an unpredictable private staging directory next to the plan and open the staged regular file exclusively. Write through its held descriptor and rename only that file. At minimum refuse every preexisting staging entry using exclusive creation rather than default truncating writes.

counterEvidence: Requires local shared-directory write and a predictable PID; no extra OS file permissions are obtained.
Intentional symlink resolution for the operator-selected plan is separate from the attacker-selected staging link.
Native Rust publication uses private UUID staging/exclusive creation but the npm path does not call it.
Dry-run skips the write.
limitations: No symlink creation or product execution was performed.
No actual shared-directory deployment was supplied; this prerequisite remains conditional.
validation.summary: No filesystem check or exclusive open lies between partial-name construction and writeFileSync. Precreation of that name can select a different victim-writable file outside the plan directory. Subsequent rename moves the staging link, after the referent has already been overwritten.

dataflow.source: Local attacker controls staging pathname entry
dataflow.outcome: Unrelated victim-writable file overwritten with plan JSON.

findings.title: A shared font-index directory permits staging symlink overwrites
findings.summary: Native font-index saving writes to a predictable PID-based temporary file with fs::write. If an operator places the index in a directory writable by a less-trusted local user, that user can redirect a cache save to another victim-writable file.

severity.rationale: Conditional local integrity impact: the default per-user directory is ordinarily trusted. Exploitation requires a configured index parent writable by another actor, PID prediction and a victim-writable referent. Document control alone is insufficient.
severity.changeConditions: A shared writable index parent makes the path applicable. Keeping the index parent private reduces exposure; exclusive regular-file staging in a private unpredictable directory removes the write primitive.

confidence.rationale: Parent confirmed arbitrary supported index configuration, cache-miss save path, predictable name and default symlink-following write. This is conditional on explicit configuration, not a claim about any actual deployment.

codeEvidence.explanation: Configured index path or parent of configured font directory determines the staging parent.

codeEvidence.explanation: Rendering a lookup not served by a current entry calls record, which saves the cache.

codeEvidence.label: Predictable temporary file is opened through fs::write
codeEvidence.explanation: A writer of a shared configured parent can plant the PID-based temp as a symlink before the default truncating write.

rootCause.summary: `font_index_path()` accepts JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX or derives the cache beside the font directory. On an uncached/stale font lookup, `indexed_faces()` records and saves entries. `FontIndex::save()` replaces the extension with tsv.PID.tmp, writes using fs::write without exclusive creation/no-follow, then renames. An existing symlink in a shared configured parent redirects the truncating write before rename.

findings.remediation: Publish the font index through an unpredictable private staging directory and an exclusively created regular file held open through writing. Atomically rename only that file; refuse preexisting staging entries and document/private-parent expectations for shared configurations.

counterEvidence: Default platform location is a per-user directory; a normal document cannot change the environment or select the index path.
JUBARTE_FONT_INDEX=off disables this sink.
Only the rendering user's existing filesystem permissions are used.
Font-family path traversal is separately guarded by a single-normal-component check.
limitations: No shared-directory deployment was supplied and no file overwrite was executed.
Browser WASM has no native font-cache filesystem path.

Real deployment evidence is not required for this conditional source path.

findings.title: Repeated HTML chunk references bypass conversion memory budgets
findings.summary: A DOCX can repeatedly reference one modest HTML part. The renderer admits the small original package, then copies and converts that chunk separately for every reference and concatenates all generated XML. The resulting allocation and work can exceed package budgets by orders of magnitude. For example, 10,000 short references to one 1 MiB ordinary HTML paragraph can imply roughly 10 GiB of generated XML; this is a static estimate, not a runtime measurement.

severity.rationale: An untrusted document supplier can choose many tiny references and one ordinary HTML part that fit original byte/depth/entry limits. The direct outcome is memory/CPU exhaustion in the embedding process or WASM instance. No service deployment is assumed; process isolation limits collateral impact.
severity.changeConditions: Shared unsandboxed upload processing increases impact; a cumulative expanded-byte/node budget enforced before append removes this path.

confidence.rationale: Parent inspected admission order, relationship load, raw HTML acceptance, per-reference conversion and unlimited output append; no runtime reproduction.

codeEvidence.explanation: The public renderer receives caller-controlled DOCX bytes and enters the shared layout path.

codeEvidence.explanation: Only the original package is admitted; relationship-selected HTML is expanded afterward and the resulting string is parsed directly.

codeEvidence.label: chunk repeat
codeEvidence.explanation: Each repeated altChunk is independently loaded and converted, and its entire WML result is appended to a growing output string without cumulative accounting.

codeEvidence.label: chunk html
codeEvidence.explanation: A normal raw HTML chunk is accepted directly, so the multiplier needs neither MIME encoding nor a malformed colspan.

codeEvidence.label: Every occurrence reloads, converts and accumulates chunk content
codeEvidence.explanation: The enclosing while loop at18 handles every reference; repeated rid values are not charged to a cumulative expanded-byte budget.

codeEvidence.label: Expanded String is parsed after admission
codeEvidence.explanation: Original-package limits do not charge each logical contribution and are not applied to generated XML before its allocation.

rootCause.summary:
`with_layout` admits only the original ZIP. `altchunk::expand` treats each reference independently, reloads the same bytes, rebuilds its HTML as WML and appends the result to one String, without a reference/output budget. The package's original bytes and entries therefore do not bound its expanded representation.
Each internal chunk occurrence adds its full converted content without cumulative import accounting. The original package-size budget applies to stored parts once, not their potentially multiplicative logical reuse.

findings.remediation: Make altChunk expansion fallible under active cumulative expanded-byte, node/element, depth, work and occurrence budgets. Check contributions before conversion/allocation/append, including repeated internal relationships and MIME-decoded chunks, and validate generated XML under active limits before DOM construction. Caching may reduce repeated conversion CPU but cannot replace the total-output budget.

counterEvidence: External URLs are not fetched; attack uses an existing internal part.
Original ZIP budget, XML depth and entry limits remain effective on stored input but not the derived repeated string.
This path needs no oversized table span and survives a per-span fix.

Verified a standard self-closing `w:altChunk r:id` form is repeatedly matched, the same existing internal relationship may be used each time, and normal HTML paragraphs can supply the repeated body. For example, thousands of small references to a roughly megabyte HTML body imply gigabytes of expanded XML although the package stores that body once.
Parent verified expand's complete per-reference loop and with_layout loader/reparse. A plain large text paragraph suffices; the operation does not depend on HTML colspan, cycles or network fetching. Conversion-result caching alone would not bound the accumulated String.

findings.summary: A drawing: image destination in ordinary Markdown is base64-decoded and deserialized into a dependency graph without validation. rootCause.summary: Imported integer-indexed dependency graphs are recursively materialized without cycle detection, node memoization or depth limits. codeEvidence.explanation: No cumulative inflated-byte or header budget is enforced.

findings.remediation: Apply bounded admission before indexing/inflation, cap cumulative header bytes, and scan incrementally. Refuse when probe budgets are exceeded.

findings.title: Rendering an admitted DOCX can retain gigabytes of duplicate embedded fonts
findings.summary: Distinct font-table aliases may all reference one embedded font part. Rendering eagerly loads every alias, copies the full font and retains a separate buffer for each name, multiplying a small admitted package into gigabytes of memory even if its body never uses those fonts.

severity.rationale: A supplier-controlled DOCX crosses the public renderer boundary under ordinary options and predictably exhausts caller memory. Source establishes process availability impact, without assuming a remote deployment or confidentiality/code-execution gain.
severity.changeConditions: Shared conversion services have greater availability impact; isolated memory-limited workers constrain host damage.

confidence.rationale: Parent review confirms unconditional loading, bytes.to_vec() per alias and distinct retained map entries. Exact exhaustion thresholds were not executed.

taxonomy.category: Unbounded expansion of shared embedded resources

codeEvidence.label: Renderer eagerly loads all embedded fonts
codeEvidence.explanation: Ordinary DOCX rendering first admits physical package bytes.

codeEvidence.label: All font table entries are loaded before run selection
codeEvidence.explanation: All embedded rows load regardless of whether body runs reference their names.

codeEvidence.label: Document supplies distinct font aliases and embedding IDs
codeEvidence.explanation: Each attacker-controlled font name and r:id creates an independent table entry.

codeEvidence.label: Deobfuscation always copies the full part
codeEvidence.explanation: Even an already plain TTF is copied before header detection; the copy is not shared by part identity.

codeEvidence.label: Every alias retains its own decoded font buffer
codeEvidence.explanation: An arbitrary family outside the installed catalogue can resolve to the same valid font part as other aliases; each is independently copied and stored.

rootCause.summary: `parse_font_table_xml()` stores attacker-selected distinct names and embedded relationship IDs. After physical package admission, `with_layout()` calls `load_embedded_fonts()` for every table row. Each unknown alias resolves the same part, calls `deobfuscate_odttf()` which immediately copies all bytes, then stores a new allocation keyed by alias/style. No resolved-part cache or aggregate decoded-font budget shares or bounds repeated copies.

findings.remediation: Cache decoded font buffers by resolved package part and effective obfuscation key, share Arc values across aliases, and enforce an aggregate decoded-font allocation/work budget before copying.

counterEvidence: Known catalogue families are skipped; use distinct unknown names.
Invalid fonts are skipped; a single valid embedded font is sufficient.
The map stores Arc values, but each iteration creates new data and a fresh Arc; there is no source-part sharing here.
ZIP byte and XML depth/attribute limits do not charge multiplicity of font aliases.
limitations: Static validation only; no exploit document or measured allocation threshold.
validation.summary: A valid ordinary font can be referenced by thousands of differently named `w:font` rows using the same `r:id`. The names need not occur in runs. Unknown family names bypass the installed-catalogue optimization and valid font parsing succeeds for every copy. Ten thousand aliases of an approximately 320 KB font request roughly 3.2 GB of retained payload bytes while archive admission charges the original part once.

codeEvidence.label: Documented redaction confidentiality promise
codeEvidence.code:
Replace the unique occurrence of ``find`` (or its ``occurrence``-th hit) with one block per character.

The redaction is no tracked change: the clean copy and the redline
both show the blocks. The plan is refused with ``REDACTION_LEAK``

repeats it.

rootCause.summary: `check_redactions()` refuses outputs only when `scrub::leaks()` finds the target. For XML attributes, `xml_holds()` ignores a matching value if its local name appears in `NUMERIC_ATTRIBUTES` and its value is hexadecimal-looking. limitations: No dynamic integration reproduction; disclosure additionally requires sharing the returned DOCX.
validation.summary: A custom XML attribute with `id=123456789` reaches the matching-value branch, passes `is_number()`, and is skipped solely because local_name is id. rootCause.summary: Admission explicitly transcodes UTF-16LE/BE with a BOM, so bounded valid property XML is accepted. The metadata scrubber's `Part::load()` instead calls `part_string()`, which interprets original bytes as UTF-8 lossily. A UTF-16 BOM becomes replacement characters, not the Unicode BOM stripped by `parse_xdocument()`. The permissive parser stops before creating a root; `Part::load()` returns `None` and `scrub_properties()` silently skips the core/app fields. Unchanged raw bytes serialize back out, while the final general-validation comparison rejects only increased findings rather than failed privacy removal.

findings.remediation: Use a shared encoding-aware XML decoder for selected metadata parts, and fail closed when a selected part cannot be parsed or requested identifying values remain. Handle both UTF-16 endiannesses consistently with admission.

counterEvidence: Valid UTF-8 property XML follows the intended removal path.
Conventional custom.xml is removed by raw existence and is not affected by this encoding-specific path.
Admission still enforces XML limits; the problem is inconsistent decoding between admission and the privacy operation.
limitations: Source validation only; no triggering document or application execution.
No Word UI behavior is asserted; original metadata bytes are recoverable by decoding the output part.
validation.method: Independent offline static encoding and control-flow trace
validation.summary: A BOM-prefixed UTF-16LE/BE `docProps/core.xml` containing creator/editor or `app.xml` containing company/manager passes admission's decoded XML check. Lossy UTF-8 creates an initial non-whitespace replacement character; the DOM root is absent and no removal runs. Even if the general validator reports a preexisting parsing finding, unchanged finding counts do not refuse `scrub()`.
